One more possibility for /ï/ is [ɪ]. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File is the Brill publisher PDF of Miyake 2018 'Studies in Pyu Phonology, ii: Rhymes' (BCL 11: 34-76, via Zenodo 3862355). The quoted passage is at the stated locator: sec. 8.1.6.2 '/ï/', running from the foot of p.44 onto p.45 (the text layer): '..schwa which is the sort of colorless vowel that might be expected in presyllables such as piṁ- in piṁṅa 'five' (4)[fn 16] and in high-frequency function words such as the realis marker ḅin·ṁḥ ~ ḅiṁḥ ~ biṁḥ and the locative marker tiṁ. iṁ may represent an unstressed reduced vowel in Indic loans: e.g., viṃṁkhno /wïk.n̥o/ 'Vishnu' (17.2) could have been pronounced [wə ˈkʰno] or [wə kʰə ˈno] with rGyalrong-style double presyllables and final stress.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated or recoverable: Pyu is extinct and attested only in Indic-script inscriptions. The describer reconstructs it as atonal and (probably) sesquisyllabic, with reduced/unstressed presyllabic vowels before a full main syllable, and speculates that polysyllabic loans had 'final stress' (iambic, main-syllable prominence) -- offered as one possibility, not a finding.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author stresses that presyllable vs. cluster readings of written CC onsets cannot yet be decided and that the phonetic value of /ï/ (schwa ~ [ɨ] ~ [ɯ] ~ [ɪ]) is open.
new_statements.domain_note: Reconstruction from orthography only; remark concerns sesquisyllabic words/Indic loanwords, not an observed prosodic system. Companion statements: Miyake 2021 sec.5 pp.40-41 ('A preinitial was probably pronounced as a presyllable with a predictable short neutral vowel after it'); Griffiths et al. 2017 sec.3.4.2 pp.143-144 ('it is most likely that Pyu was atonal at the time it was first written').
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe epigraphic Pyu (Tircul) of Upper Burma, glottocode burm1262 / ISO pyx, as a single written language spanning c. 6th-13th c. CE; Miyake notes the uniform orthography may hide dialectal and diachronic variation. Not to be confused with the Papuan language Pyu (Kwomtari region).

sources.locator: sec. 8.1.6.2 '/ï/', p. 45 (with abstract p. 34 and sec. 5 p. 38)
sources.note: Abstract and sec.10: Pyu was atonal (dots = /ä ï/ and fricatives, not tones; possibly tones later). Sec.5 p.38: sesquisyllabic /(C).(C)V(C)/ with possibly 'a short unstressed vowel' between preinitial and initial. Sec.8.1.6.2 p.45: /ï/ may be a schwa-like presyllabic/unstressed reduced vowel; 'Vishnu' could have been [wə ˈkʰno] or [wə kʰə ˈno] 'with rGyalrong-style double presyllables and final stress' -- the only locational stress remark, explicitly speculative.

sources.note: Sec.5 pp.38-41: Pyu was probably sesquisyllabic; 'A preinitial was probably pronounced as a presyllable with a predictable short neutral vowel after it'; structure /(C).(C)V(C)/ ~ /(C)(ə)(C)V(C)/. No explicit stress rule; tone/register question deferred to Miyake 2018.

sources.note: Sec.3.4.1-3.4.2 pp.143-144: maximal written syllable <C1C2C3VC4 ṃṁḥ>; 'it is most likely that Pyu was atonal at the time it was first.. though the language may have developed registers or even tones later'. Nothing on word stress beyond calling tiṁ a possible 'unstressed form' of tva and pliṁ an 'unstressed [ɨ]-like vowel' in a compound.
